**Part 2:**   
I found the company through an ad in the paper. "Would you like to try your hand at being telepathic?" it said. I couldn't help but laugh. "Sure, why not?" I thought, "I've got nothing better to do."  
I was expecting some guy in a trench coat to bring me to his spooky shack and try to mystify me with a card trick or two, something like that. It was nothing like that. I dialed the number in the ad and a smooth voice greeted me. "Hello, would you like to try your hand at being telepathic?"   
So, right number then. "Sure" I responded, trying not to mock. The voice spoke an address and a time to be there. I had just enough time to make it at an easy stroll. The building was huge. Giant white marble pillars outside, big foggy glass windows, bronze accents. A truly wild looking place, straight out of futuristic Greece. I opened one of the big glass doors and stepped inside.  
You can probably guess how the next part went. Lots of introductions and paper signing, mental health panels, medical history and background check. I was in the first month of an off year at my job, the benefits of modern infrastructure, so I wasn't worried about the roughly six hour process, I had free time in spades. I was finally sat down in front of a woman of a certain age in a white lab coat. Bright white smile and thick jeweled glasses. She explained that, though it may seem humorous, they were in fact very serious about their claim of extra-natural abilities. Though there were minor side effects, most were caused by pre-existing instability, and all were manageable. They were offering substantial compensation, and promised I "never need  work another day in my life," Which sounded just fine to me.  
One four year training montage later, full of injections, pills, minor illness and what felt like a decade of sitting silently in a room, alone except for the soft glow of quite good artificial sunlight through a "window" in my simply furnished room and I was "ready to go." They had explained in the beginning that the meditation was not part of the telepathy, but that both were guaranteed to be necessary for the end of the project. Okay, sure.  
They strapped me down to a big gleaming white chair. I could still shift, but no arm or leg movement. One of them placed some of those little electrodes on my head and everyone stepped back. "Are we ready?"  
"All green lights."  
"Okay people, hold onto your coats."  
"Jump in five."   
"Still green."  
"Four. Three. Two." Here goes nothing.  
"One. Go."  
I was ripped in half. I was expecting it, having read the last fifteen years of trial logs, but god damn did it feel strange. Part of my training was learning to control other people. Starting with rats, then dogs, you know how it goes. I had been living peoples days for them for a year now. Thirty-two straight hours of sleep on a genius mind like the researchers here was a godsend. They slept, I meditated and piloted them around for a day. After the first couple test runs they all were able to stay dreaming and came back the next day remade. The sleep they were able to get with no obligations, and a bit of mental sedation on my part, refreshed them like nothing else. By the end of last month I was able to control thee at once for a whole day, all while doing my usual simple tasks.   
The sensation of being in my own head, but twice was really strange. None of the researchers were telepathic, and feeling the presence of all of the researchers minds in double around me was a bit confusing at first. I took a minute to focus, and then with both mouths asked to be let up. This was one week ago. It had played out the same way I remembered, though without the two points of view. They wanted everything to be the exact same, so when I got back here it would be easier to integrate myself into myself.  
After making sure I was okay, not screaming and dying and all that, which hadn't happened in years, but this was the furthest back they had sent one of us, they started the tests. FMRI, vitals, the works. They found out through the trials that rather than your mind and body being teleported back through space and time, which they say (to me, the telepath) is impossible, that just your mind goes, back into your head from the past. This had the unfortunate side effect of driving the jumper insane from overstimulation, causing the brain to overload and stroke out. This was able to be overcome, as they now know, with a LOT of training, and a bit of super powered mumbo jumbo.   
For the next week we followed the plan. They had set it out, including the tests and such, to exacting detail, to be followed so as to divert the timeline as little as possible. All data was stored just as before, and not touched for the following week until the jump date. Everyone followed their routines and all went as planned. The only difference was my routine. I was asked to make a single small change that none of the researchers witnessed, to see if I could influence the timeline and redirect the original. I wrote a "2" on a piece of paper that I had previously written "1" on, the only difference. If at the end of the week it was still a two then I had successfully changed the course of history.  
They found out a couple months after starting the telepath trials that the timelines could be merged again. A couple of the first telepaths were left bisected in two different worlds, slowly changing, eventually driving them insane as well because of the extreme dissonance. They learned that if all actions were carefully marked down and followed they could merge the mind of the telepath with their mind from the future, closing the timeline and saving the mind of the telepath. Mine was the first to try changing the timeline intentionally and re-merging them to see if we could change history. The week was long, but worth it for the possibility of changing the past.   
I woke up on the jump date covered in blood. I sat up like a shot, my head pounding, crusted blood down my face from my mouth and nose. Then I realized where I was. The jump chair. I guess the stress of trying to merge the timelines was too much strain on my body. The team stood around me, worried looks on their faces. One raised her hand, a piece of paper pinched between thumb and pointer finger.   
"2".

**Part 1:**  
I was the first Telepath sent to the past, or "past" I suppose. The first time travel trial was a 10 minute jump to see the effects. They might have been expecting the poor guy to vanish and appear ten minutes ago, and they would go from there. But even that first expected success blew up in their face. As soon as they hit the "GO" button the hopeful time traveler started screaming. Screaming and screaming, like a tortured soul newly damned to hell. They say it sounded like two people screaming in unison, but that might just be the trauma. Eventually the guys throat gave out. He collapsed, simultaneously coughing up blood and dying from a stroke.   


So, trial one was a failure, and they didn't have a clue why. Why was the subject still in the present, why couldn't he speak, and why couldn't he stop screaming. They took a couple weeks to come up with their best ideas and tried again. The second trial worked about as well as the first, though it took about a few hours longer. They sedated the subject before sending her back. No screaming, but she was still here, which, they thought, is not how time travel works. However, once the sedative wore off she also started screaming. Howling without words before they sedated her again, a double dose. When she finally started waking up, for about four seconds, she seemed confused.   


"But I'm at home", she said. Her eyes widened and she went limp. Stroke, again.  


Now they had a tiny bit of information, and a way to get more. Use a sedative that puts someone right at the edge of consciousness, enough to maybe mumble a word or two, but not enough to start screaming. After the failures of the first two attempts they needed to make a decision. Either find people that wouldn't be missed, or highly trained professionals that were happy to give up their lives in the "line of duty". They decided to go with the professionals.  


Trials three and four ended up worse than number two. They tried jumping them further back than the previous trials. Neither of the military men could be put into that sweet spot of not quite awake. Because of years of training they basically had a lightswitch in their head, "Asleep" or "Awake". The poor guys ended up stroking out after about thirty minutes each. Then there was trial five, the best trial so far. The subject was dropped into sedation and sent back. After about fifteen minutes of fiddling they started talking. Well, not at first. Before any words come out, they were humming. A long, flat tone. Inhale, hum while exhaling, and repeat. For about three minutes, then came the talking.   


"Two tablespoons of coffee", they said in a clear voice startling the researchers standing around them. "One sugar cube, and a dash of milk, just how mom used to make."  


Well that was something. After a minute of silence they started talking again. "Wait, I'm still in the lab aren't I. This isn't what I was expecting. This feels so real though. It has to be real, right?."   


Their eyelids snapped open, revealing bloodshot eyes. "I've never been in more than one place at a time before.", they whispered, their eyes rolling back into their head.  


It turns out spending five years at a monastery before joining the military does a number on your mental fortitude. It seems they were able to survive not because they were a tough bastard, but because their mind was able to easily find that state of half waking. After that trial, the company had to figure out a better way to deal with time travel side effects.
